content: The studies conducted by Selwyn et al. and Moss et al. were prospective in nature and focused on high-risk populations, such as intravenous drug users (IVDU) with HIV infection and homeless individuals, respectively. These studies were performed during a time when antiretroviral therapy (ART) was not available. Both studies had significant limitations, including small sample sizes, lack of control for confounding variables, and no tuberculosis (TB) cases observed in the control arm of the Selwyn study. The quality of evidence was rated as very low. Moran-Mendoza et al. conducted a large population-based study examining the relationship between tuberculin skin test (TST) size and the risk of developing TB among contacts of contagious TB cases. The study defined TB incidence based on smearor culture-positive results, histopathological diagnosis, or clinical and radiological diagnosis of active TB when smear and culture results were negative. However, the study had limitations, including the use of casual contacts as a proxy for the general population in the control arm, lack of control for confounders, and removal of some TST-positive individuals who opted for isoniazid (INH) treatment, introducing self-selection bias. The quality of evidence was rated as very low. Christopoulos et al. conducted a prospective multicenter clinical trial to identify risk factors for TB in dialysis patients. The control arm consisted of an age-matched group from health service registries, but it was unclear whether the controls were selected based on positive purified protein derivative (PPD) status. Adjusted relative risk (Adj RR) was calculated to account for other characteristics, but the study did not specify whether the control group was PPD-positive. The quality of evidence was rated as very low. Ferebee reviewed controlled chemoprophylaxis trials in TB, including one trial among contacts of active TB cases and another among patients in mental hospitals. The analysis compared TB incidence in skin converters during 12 months of placebo treatment with PPD-positive controls at entry, with follow-up extending to three years for each cohort. The study highlighted the lack of control for confounders and the potential for survival bias. The quality of evidence was rated as low. Edwards et al. examined the relationship between height, weight, and TB infection in a cohort of U.S. Navy recruits from 1958 to 1967. Underweight recruits were defined as those weighing more than 10% below the median weight for their height, while overweight recruits were defined as those weighing more than 10% above the median. The study presented morbidity rates as cases per 100,000 men tested but did not control for confounders. Additionally, height and weight data were self-reported, increasing the risk of misclassification. The quality of evidence was rated as very low. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) system was used to assess the certainty of evidence. High-quality evidence indicates a very good indication of the likely effect, with a low likelihood of substantial differences. Moderate-quality evidence provides a good indication of the likely effect, with a moderate likelihood of substantial differences. Low-quality evidence offers some indication of the likely effect, but the likelihood of substantial differences is high. Very low-quality evidence does not provide a reliable indication of the likely effect, with a very high likelihood of substantial differences. The diagnosis of latent TB infection (LTBI) relies on indirect tests such as TST and interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs), which measure memory T-cell responses to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens. While TST is inexpensive and widely used, it has poor specificity in Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG)-vaccinated populations and immunocompromised individuals. IGRAs have better specificity but are more costly and require specialized laboratory equipment. Both tests have poor positive predictive value (PPV) for the development of active TB, and it remains unclear which test is preferable for identifying high-risk individuals for LTBI treatment. Before initiating LTBI treatment, active TB must be excluded to avoid ineffective treatment and the risk of fostering drug resistance. Screening methods, including symptom assessment and chest radiography, have variable sensitivity and specificity depending on the population and setting. The systematic review of screening methods identified heterogeneity in pooled estimates, particularly between studies from sub-Saharan Africa (high HIV prevalence) and Asian populations (low HIV prevalence but high smoking prevalence). This variability underscores the need for tailored approaches to screening and diagnosis in different settings. An appropriate algorithm is required to identify individuals in high-risk groups who would benefit most from LTBI treatment. This algorithm should include tests to diagnose TB infection (rule-in) and investigations to exclude active TB disease (rule-out). Both TST and IGRAs have moderate-to-high sensitivity and specificity for LTBI diagnosis but low predictive value for future TB development. The performance of these tests should be evaluated based on incidence rate ratios and PPV for active TB development.
